yak.origin: Yak fiber comes from the domestic yak, Bos grunniens, a bovine of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau whose dense coat is a key cold adaptation; herds sampled in one Sichuan study lived at roughly 3,100 to 4,200 m. The coat is layered: coarse outer hair, including the long flank or skirt hair that distinguishes yak from other cattle, over a fine down. Breeds differ in color, and the Tianzhu White Yak is studied specifically for hair yield and length. Reliable global volume figures for yak down could not be verified here.
yak.structure: Yak down and hair are keratin fibers with a cuticle, cortex and, in coarser fibers, a medulla. The down resembles cashmere closely enough that the two are hard to separate by appearance; an untargeted proteomic survey identified 156 proteins in yak, 174 in cashmere and 157 in wool fibers, with substantial sequence homology among them. Most yak fiber is naturally dark because of melanin granules in the cortex. Unpigmented belly hair studied as a model showed higher porosity than human hair at every structural level, a lower Young's modulus, smaller intermediate filament spacing and fewer overlapping cuticle scales, features that ease dye uptake.
yak.process: The coat follows a seasonal cycle of anagen, catagen and telogen, with WNT and FGF signaling active in growth and BMP and DKK1 signals in regression, so down is collected around the molt. Raw fiber is scoured and dehaired to separate down from outer hair, as with cashmere. Because most fiber is brown or black, pale shades require bleaching: one study used a melanin-targeted Fenton process in which iron ions bound to melanin catalyze hydrogen peroxide decomposition, and ultrasound raised the whiteness index from 11 to 45 with about 15% loss of tensile strength. Bleached or natural fiber is then carded and spun.
yak.performance: Dehaired yak down behaves like other fine keratin: hygroscopic, warm when slightly damp, self-extinguishing in flame and receptive to acid dyes, although its natural brown limits the palette unless bleached, and bleaching partly cleaves disulfide bonds and roughens the cuticle. Fine down in lightly twisted yarn pills and abrades more readily than long worsted wool, and residual outer hair raises prickle and coarsens the handle. Like all protein fibers it needs protection from clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae, and alkaline washing weakens it.
yak.identify: Burn tests (indicative only, and to be done with care) cannot separate yak from wool or cashmere. Microscopy of scale pattern and diameter is the accepted commercial method but depends on the operator. Species-specific keratin peptides measured by LC/ESI-MS or by targeted parallel reaction monitoring distinguish yak, wool and cashmere and can quantify blends, even in chemically treated fabric. ATR-FTIR with chemometrics and MALDI-TOF peptide profiling have also separated yak from other specialty hairs. Undeclared yak in cashmere is the main labeling risk.
yak.labeling: Yak is not among the specialty fibers named in the US Wool Products Labeling Act, so its content is disclosed under the textile rules: 16 CFR 303.6 allows the animal's name with the word hair, fiber or blend, for example yak hair, when the fiber is 5% or more of the product, or the collective term fur fiber when no claim about the animal is made. Yak must never be labeled cashmere. In the EU, Annex I of Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 lists yak among the named fine animal hairs, followed or not by wool or hair.
yak.past: Yak coats have long served plateau pastoralists, while the fine down reached international knitwear markets more recently through industrial dehairing. Much current research is Chinese and genomic: single-cell and transcriptome atlases of yak hair follicles and genome-wide association studies of hair weight and length in the Tianzhu White Yak are framed explicitly as ways to make fuller use of yak fiber and support pastoral economies. Researchers also describe yak hair as a widely available but underexploited dark fiber, and have tested byproduct uses such as bioplastic films made from discarded hair.
